title: Spies and judges: how MI5 avoided prosecution for contempt of court?
gist: Legal commentary criticising a High Court decision that it was not in the public interest to hold MI5 officers in contempt of court despite findings that MI5 lied to the court; the author argues most of the court's reasons are unconvincing and that the ruling effectively forecloses any CPS prosecution, undermining the rule of law over security services.

themes.theme: High Court declines to hold MI5 in contempt

insights.claim: The High Court ruled that it was not in the public interest to hold MI5 officers in contempt of court even though there had been lies to the court.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Sets a precedent limiting judicial sanction of UK security services; relevant to rule-of-law and civil-liberties risk assessments.

insights.claim: Further proceedings against MI5 are unlikely because the security services benefit from wide statutory exemptions and from the public-interest test the Crown Prosecution Service must apply.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Expect no prosecution to follow; accountability of UK intelligence agencies remains weak.
